relevance_note: The paper describes five Blau syndrome subjects with NOD2 substitutions listed per person in Table 1 ("| **#1** | 50 | M | R334W | Prednisone") plus two case reports.
method_note: Read by hand; a short script assembled the JSON from my reading and the spans were checked verbatim against the paper. Table 1 lists healthy controls (out of scope, no rows) and Blau syndrome subjects #1-#5 in a column of bare numbers, labelled 'Table 1 #n'. Subject #5 is also called 'subject 5' and is the patient of the case report headed 'Case 1' ('A 27 year old female (subject 5 in the cytokine synthesis study above)'); I used the label 'Case 1' for her. Table 1 gives her age as 30 while Case 1 opens at age 27 and the narrative then spans several further years; I recorded 30 (age in Table 1, at the study) as age at last evaluation, which may not be her age at the latest case-report follow-up. Families: 'Subjects one, two and three include a mother and two sons; subjects four and five represent a mother and her son.' The paper does not say which of #1-#3 is the mother; #2 is the only female (68 F), so I took her as the mother and recorded inherited maternal for #1 and #3 (sons, R334W like #2) and for #4 (son of #5, both R334Q). This identification of the mother is inferred from sex and age; the paper gives no family labels. Case 1's 'son, who also has Blau syndrome' was taken to be subject #4 (from 'subjects four and five represent a mother and her son'); no separate row. Case 2 (17-year-old male, not in the cytokine study) has no NOD2 genotype given, so no variant row. R334W/R334Q are printed as protein short forms without 'p.'; recorded as printed in variant_original_string and protein_hgvs_as_stated; no cDNA, transcript or zygosity printed. Variant type left 'not reported' ('NOD2 substitution' column header and 'nonsynonymous substitutions' are general). Functional evidence (PBMC cytokine assays) is stated for the named group of five subjects and copied to each. Subjects #1-#4 have no individual clinical features (only 'classical manifestations of Blau syndrome'), so their checklists are all 'not reported'. A previously published Blau syndrome patient is described with individual-level facts (elevated serum IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα that normalized on anakinra; persistence of ocular symptoms; novel NOD2 mutation). The Introduction cites this as (34) (Arostegui 2007, Spanish cohort), while the Discussion cites a matching description ('one Blau syndrome case with elevated serum IL-1β', 'a Spanish group ... one Blau syndrome patient with a novel mutation in NOD2') as (8), which in the reference list is Agostini 2004 (NALP3 inflammasome), apparently a citation error in the paper. I treated these as one person, 'ref (34) patient', with a variant row 'not reported'; this merge is a judgement. Case 1: cataract not recorded although she had bilateral lensectomies (cataract not stated). Visual impairment marked observed from reduced visual acuity and visual field constriction (Case 1) and from an enucleated left eye plus 20/50+1 OD (Case 2). cohort_size_as_stated = 5 Blau syndrome subjects (plus five healthy controls, not counted). No contradictions found apart from the age 27 vs 30 difference and the (8)/(34) citation mismatch.

treatment_summary.value: Systemic medication at study: etanercept and methotrexate. History of high-dose prednisone, rofecoxib, gold injections, cyclosporine, periocular corticosteroid injections and infliximab (reportedly effective, stopped for cost); methotrexate 25 mg weekly plus etanercept; daily anakinra 100 mg/day for about 6 weeks, ineffective and discontinued; back to etanercept and methotrexate; currently methotrexate 25mg/week, prednisone 5mg QD and Naprosyn 500mg QD with omeprazole.
span: **#5** | 30 | F | R334Q | Etanercept, methotrexate

She reported taking a high daily dose of prednisone for many years. She had also tried various treatments including rofecoxib, gold injections, cyclosporine, periocular corticosteroid injections, and infliximab.
She eventually tolerated a regimen of methotrexate injections, 25 mg weekly, and etanercept, with periodic oral or periocular corticosteroids for flares.
Approximately 6 weeks after starting anakinra, it was evident that it was ineffective and was discontinued. She was switched back to etanercept and remained on methotrexate.
her eyes and joints are doing well on a regimen consisting of methotrexate 25mg/week, prednisone 5mg QD, and Naprosyn 500mg QD along with daily omeprazole for GI protection

span: was being treated with infliximab infusions, 5–10 mg/kg every 4–6 weeks
Topical brimonidine TID, topical timolol/dorzolamide BID, and acetazolamide 125 mg to 250 mg PO TID were required for control of intraocular pressure.
Despite the use of methylprednisolone (10–25 mg/day) and cyclosporine (up to 5 mg/kg/day) along with anakinra, inflammation remained after 2 months of therapy
Anakinra was discontinued and treatment with adalimumab was substituted. Prednisolone and cyclosporine were continued. Within 1 month, inflammation was improved.
